How Are Bonuses Taxed? The 22% Withholding Rule, Take-Home Math, and the Refund Test

Direct AnswerA $10,000 bonus at a $65,000 salary keeps $7,035 after 22% federal withholding and FICA, and $150 comes back at tax time. Both methods and the 2026 refund test.

Gross pay estimates

Quick Answer

A $10,000 bonus at a $65,000 salary keeps $7,035 on payday: $2,200 federal withholding at the flat 22% supplemental rate, plus $620 Social Security and $145 Medicare. But the real federal tax on that bonus is only $2,050 — so $150 comes back when you file, and the bonus is truly worth $7,185. The 22% is withholding, not your tax rate.

The Short Answer: $7,035 of a $10,000 Bonus

A $10,000 bonus paid to a single filer earning $65,000 a year keeps $7,035 after federal withholding and FICA — 70.35% of the bonus — when there is no state tax and wages are below the Social Security wage base. The federal withholding is a flat 22% ($2,200), Social Security takes 6.2% ($620), and Medicare takes 1.45% ($145). Because that worker's real marginal rate on the bonus is a mix of 12% and 22%, the actual federal tax is $2,050, so $150 of the withholding returns as part of the tax refund.

That gap between what is withheld and what is owed is the whole story of bonus tax, and this guide prices every part of it: the two withholding methods your employer can choose, the take-home ladder for every bonus size, the refund-or-bill test by marginal rate, the Social Security wage-base crossing, the 37% rule above $1 million, the 401(k) deferral trade, and the bonus-versus-raise comparison. All figures use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction, federal only unless a section says otherwise. Our FICA guide explains the 7.65% layer in detail, and our pay-stub guide shows where each of these lines appears on your check.

What Counts as a Bonus for Tax Purposes

The IRS does not tax bonuses under a special “bonus tax.” It calls them supplemental wages — pay that is not regular wages for a pay period — and the same label covers performance bonuses, year-end bonuses, signing bonuses, commissions, severance pay, back pay, and stock awards paid in cash. A gift card or a prize from your employer is also taxable compensation; it is just usually added to a regular paycheck instead of being paid separately.

Two consequences follow from the label. First, the bonus is ordinary income: it lands on your W-2 in Box 1 with your salary, it is taxed at your normal brackets, and it counts toward your total income for credits, the standard deduction phase-outs, and everything else. Second, your employer is allowed to withhold federal income tax from it using a flat supplemental rate instead of your W-4 tables — which is where the 22% comes from. The label changes the withholding mechanics, not the final tax.

The Three Federal Withholding Rates on Bonuses

Federal withholding on a bonus is one of three numbers, depending on how the bonus is paid and how large it is:

22%

Percentage method

Flat 22% federal withholding on separately paid bonuses, up to $1 million of supplemental wages in the year. The default for most employers.

Your W-4 rate

Aggregate method

Bonus combined with your regular paycheck and run through the W-4 tables. Usually withholds a little more — $50.54 more on a $5,000 bonus in our worked example.

37%

Above $1 million

Mandatory 37% withholding on the part of the year's supplemental wages above $1 million. Only the excess is taxed at 37%, never the whole bonus.

Your employer picks the method, not you — and the choice is made per payment, so the same employer can use the percentage method for a separately paid year-end bonus and the aggregate method for a bonus folded into a regular paycheck. Either way, the method changes only what is withheld on the day. Your final tax is computed from total income at filing, which is why the same bonus can feel over-taxed in December and then partly return in April.

What Actually Gets Taken Out of a Bonus

Five layers can come off a bonus before it reaches your bank account. Federal withholding is the only one with a special bonus rate; the rest work exactly as they do on regular pay:

LayerRate (2026)On a $10,000 bonusNotes
Federal income tax withholding22% flat (37% above $1M)$2,200.00Withholding, not final tax — reconciled at filing
Social Security6.2%$620.00Stops at the $184,500 wage base
Medicare1.45%$145.00No cap; +0.9% above $200,000 in wages
State income tax withholding0% – ~11.7%$0 – $1,170.00Depends on your state (see below)
Retirement / benefitsVaries$0 if none elected401(k) deferrals reduce income-tax wages, not FICA

State withholding deserves its own look because the range is wide. Nine states have no income tax at all, so nothing extra comes off. Flat-tax states withhold at their flat rate — Illinois at 4.95%, for example. And a few high-tax states set their own supplemental rate for bonuses: California withholds 10.23% on bonuses and stock options (6.6% on other supplemental pay), and New York withholds around 11.7%, with New York City adding roughly 4.25% local withholding on top. On a $5,000 bonus, California takes another $511.50, leaving $3,006.00 instead of the $3,517.50 a no-tax-state worker keeps. State rates are withholding rates, not final tax rates — verify yours with your state revenue department, because a state can also simply apply your normal W-4 tables instead of a flat supplemental rate.

The Percentage Method: A $10,000 Bonus, Step by Step

The percentage method is the one most workers meet: the bonus is paid separately (or identified separately on the pay stub), and the employer withholds a flat 22% for federal income tax. Here is the full journey of a $10,000 year-end bonus for a single filer earning $65,000, no state tax, wages below the Social Security wage base:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Federal withholding$10,000 × 22%−$2,200.00
Step 2 — Social Security$10,000 × 6.2%−$620.00
Step 3 — Medicare$10,000 × 1.45%−$145.00
Step 4 — Take-home on payday$10,000 − $2,200 − $620 − $145$7,035.00 (70.35%)
Step 5 — Actual federal tax on the bonus$7,670 on $75,000 − $5,620 on $65,000$2,050.00
Step 6 — Refund at filing$2,200 withheld − $2,050 owed$150.00 back
Step 7 — True value of the bonus$10,000 − $2,050 − $765 FICA$7,185.00

Step 5 is where the money is. The worker's taxable income without the bonus is $48,900 ($65,000 minus the $16,100 standard deduction), and the 12% bracket runs to $50,400 — so the first $1,500 of the bonus is taxed at 12% ($180) and the remaining $8,500 at 22% ($1,870), for $2,050 total. The employer withheld 22% on all $10,000, including the $1,500 slice that only owed 12% — that $150 over-withholding is exactly the refund. The same arithmetic explains why the refund is $150 for any bonus of $1,500 or more at this salary, and $100 for a $1,000 bonus (12% of $1,000 is $120, withheld $220). The honesty note: this refund arrives months later, as part of your whole return — do not spend it in December.

The Aggregate Method: The Same Bonus, a Different Paycheck

Under the aggregate method the employer adds the bonus to your regular paycheck and runs the combined amount through the W-4 withholding tables (IRS Publication 15-T). The federal withholding attributed to the bonus is the difference between the withholding on the combined check and the withholding on the regular check alone. Same worker, same $5,000 bonus, paid biweekly at a $65,000 salary — $2,500 a regular check:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Federal on the regular check$5,620 annual tax ÷ 26 checks$216.15
Step 2 — Combined check$2,500 regular + $5,000 bonus$7,500.00
Step 3 — Federal on the combined check$35,534 annual tax on $195,000 ÷ 26$1,366.69
Step 4 — Federal attributed to the bonus$1,366.69 − $216.15$1,150.54 (23.01%)
Step 5 — FICA on the bonus$310 Social Security + $72.50 Medicare$382.50
Step 6 — Take-home on payday$5,000 − $1,150.54 − $382.50$3,466.96
Step 7 — Compared with the percentage method$3,517.50 − $3,466.96$50.54 less in hand

Why does the aggregate method take more? The tables annualize the combined check — $7,500 biweekly looks like a $195,000 salary — so part of the bonus is withheld as if it sat in the 24% bracket, even though the worker's real year ends at $70,000 in the 22% bracket. The $50.54 is still just withholding: at filing, the actual federal tax on this $5,000 bonus is $950, so the worker gets back $200.54 of the $1,150.54 — a bigger refund than the $150 under the percentage method, for the same true value of $3,667.50. Two practical points: the aggregate method is most common at smaller employers and when a bonus is folded into a regular pay period, and the exact cents depend on your W-4 — payroll software follows the published tables, so your figure may differ by a few dollars. If your bonus check looks wildly over-taxed, check your pay stub first: the aggregate method is usually the explanation, not an error. Our pay-stub guide shows how to spot which method was used.

Every Bonus Size, Same Salary: The Take-Home Ladder

Same worker ($65,000 salary, single filer, no state tax, below the Social Security wage base), six bonus sizes. The payday take-home is always 70.35% of the bonus under the percentage method — because 22% plus 7.65% FICA is a flat 29.65% — but the true value after the refund is a little higher, and the refund is always the same $150 once the bonus passes $1,500:

Bonus (gross)Federal withheld (22%)FICA (7.65%)Take-home on paydayActual federal taxRefundTrue value
$1,000$220.00$76.50$703.50$120.00$100.00$803.50
$2,500$550.00$191.25$1,758.75$400.00$150.00$1,908.75
$5,000$1,100.00$382.50$3,517.50$950.00$150.00$3,667.50
$10,000 (anchor)$2,200.00$765.00$7,035.00$2,050.00$150.00$7,185.00
$25,000$5,500.00$1,912.50$17,587.50$5,350.00$150.00$17,737.50
$50,000$11,000.00$3,825.00$35,175.00$10,850.00$150.00$35,325.00

The flat $150 refund is not a coincidence. At a $65,000 salary, taxable income is $48,900 and the 12% bracket tops out at $50,400 — so exactly $1,500 of any bonus is taxed at 12% instead of 22%, and 10% of $1,500 is $150. Raise the salary and the refund shrinks: at $70,000 the taxable income is already $53,900, past the 12% bracket's top, so every bonus dollar is taxed at 22% and the refund is zero. Lower the salary and the refund grows: at $52,000, the whole $5,000 bonus sits in the 12% bracket, so $500 of the $1,100 withheld comes back. The ladder's lesson is that “22% of my bonus” is never the final answer — your salary sets the refund.

Refund or Bill? Your Marginal Rate Decides

The reconciliation at filing is a single comparison: the 22% withheld against your actual marginal rate on the bonus dollars. Three outcomes, each with a worked example from this guide:

Your marginal rate on the bonusWithheldResult at filingWorked example in this guide
10% or 12%22%Refund — 10 or 12 points back$52,000 salary + $5,000 bonus: $500 back
22%22%Break even — nothing back, nothing owed$70,000 salary + $5,000 bonus: $0
24% or higher22%Bill — 2 to 15 points owed$150,000 salary + $30,000 bonus: $600 owed

The $52,000 example shows the refund side at its clearest. Salary $52,000, taxable income $35,900, federal tax $4,060. Add a $5,000 bonus: taxable income $40,900, federal tax $4,660. The bonus's real federal tax is $600 — the whole $5,000 sits in the 12% bracket — but the employer withheld $1,100, so $500 returns. The $150,000 example shows the other side: salary $150,000, taxable income $133,900, federal tax $24,734; with a $30,000 bonus the taxable income is $163,900 and the tax is $31,934, so the bonus's real federal tax is $7,200 — but only $6,600 was withheld, leaving a $600 bill. That worker's take-home on the bonus was $21,105 ($30,000 minus $6,600 federal, $1,860 Social Security, and $435 Medicare), and the $600 is due at filing. The fix for the second case is in the section below — do it in December, not April.

Social Security, Medicare, and the $184,500 Line

FICA has no bonus exception: Social Security at 6.2% and Medicare at 1.45% apply to bonus pay exactly as they do to salary. What changes with a bonus is timing — a December bonus often arrives when the year's wages are near or past the Social Security wage base of $184,500, and that changes the math in your favor:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Year-to-date Social Security wagesSalary already paid$182,500.00
Step 2 — Room left under the wage base$184,500 − $182,500$2,000.00
Step 3 — Social Security on the $5,000 bonus$2,000 × 6.2% (rest is above the base)$124.00
Step 4 — Medicare on the bonus$5,000 × 1.45% (no cap)$72.50
Step 5 — Federal withholding$5,000 × 22%$1,100.00
Step 6 — Take-home on payday$5,000 − $1,100 − $124 − $72.50$3,703.50
Step 7 — Compared with a bonus under the base$3,703.50 − $3,517.50$186.00 more kept

Two Medicare details catch people out. The regular 1.45% has no cap, so it applies to the whole bonus at any income. And the additional 0.9% Medicare tax starts once an employer's wages to you pass $200,000 in the calendar year — your employer must withhold it from that point on, regardless of your filing status, even though your final liability uses $200,000 for single filers and $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. A worker with two jobs can therefore be under-withheld on the additional Medicare tax, because neither employer sees the other's wages. If your bonus pushes total wages past $200,000, expect the extra 0.9% on the part above the line — $45 on a $5,000 bonus that crosses it — and check the combined figure at filing.

Bonuses Over $1 Million: The 37% Rule

Once your supplemental wages from one employer pass $1 million in a calendar year, the withholding rate on the excess is a mandatory 37% — the top federal bracket. The threshold is cumulative across every supplemental payment from that employer in the year, not per bonus, and only the dollars above $1 million are withheld at 37%. A $1,200,000 bonus year for an executive already earning a $250,000 salary (past both the Social Security wage base and the $200,000 additional-Medicare line) works out like this: federal withholding is $220,000 on the first $1 million at 22%, plus $74,000 on the $200,000 above it at 37% — $294,000 total. Social Security is $0, because the wage base was already cleared by the salary. Medicare is $17,400 (1.45% of $1,200,000) plus $10,800 additional Medicare (0.9% of $1,200,000). Total withheld: $322,200, leaving $877,800. The 37% tier rarely produces a refund, because it is close to the marginal rate such earners actually pay — but the FICA treatment still matters: a bonus that arrives before the wage base is cleared would lose another 6.2% on the part below $184,500.

Putting the Bonus in Your 401(k): What It Actually Saves

Deferring part of a bonus into a traditional 401(k) is the one lever that changes the tax on a bonus before payday — but it works differently from what most people assume. The deferral reduces the wages subject to federal income-tax withholding, so the 22% applies to the smaller amount. It does not reduce FICA wages: Social Security and Medicare still apply to the full bonus. On our $10,000 anchor bonus, deferring 10% ($1,000):

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Deferral to 401(k)10% × $10,000$1,000.00
Step 2 — Federal withholding22% × ($10,000 − $1,000)$1,980.00 (was $2,200)
Step 3 — FICA (unchanged)7.65% × $10,000$765.00
Step 4 — Cash in hand$10,000 − $1,000 − $1,980 − $765$6,255.00 (was $7,035)
Step 5 — Net position$6,255 cash + $1,000 in 401(k)$220 ahead overall

The $220 is the federal tax you did not pay on the deferred $1,000 — it is deferred, not eliminated, and it will be taxed when you withdraw it in retirement. Three practical limits: the election must be made before the bonus is paid (you cannot reclassify money already received), some plans cap the percentage you may defer from a bonus or exclude bonuses from deferrals entirely, and the deferral counts toward the annual 401(k) contribution limit. If your employer matches contributions, check whether the match applies to bonus deferrals too — a match on the $1,000 would make the trade better still. Run the exact trade on the 401(k) paycheck impact calculator before electing.

Bonus vs Raise: The Same $5,000, Very Different Value

A $5,000 bonus and a $5,000 raise look like the same money. In the first year they are — to the dollar. A single filer at $65,000 who gets a $5,000 raise to $70,000 takes home $58,075 instead of $54,407.50: $3,667.50 more a year. The same worker's $5,000 bonus, after its $950 of real federal tax and $382.50 of FICA, is also worth $3,667.50. The difference is what happens in year two:

Measure$5,000 bonus (one time)$5,000 raise (permanent)Limitation
Year 1 after-tax value$3,667.50$3,667.50Identical — same brackets, same FICA
Year 2 after-tax value$0$3,667.50Bonus must be earned again
5-year after-tax value$3,667.50$18,337.50Before future raises compound on the higher base
Next raise is calculated on$65,000 base$70,000 baseA 3% raise is $150/yr bigger on the higher base
401(k) match / PTO accrualUsually no effectUsually rises with base payDepends on plan rules — check before deciding
RiskNone — already earnedNone once grantedA promised bonus can shrink; a granted raise cannot

The negotiation lesson follows directly: when an employer offers a bonus instead of a raise, price it as one year of the raise, not as the raise itself. A $5,000 bonus in place of a $5,000 raise costs $14,670 over five years before compounding. That does not make bonuses bad — a bonus on top of a raise is the best of both, and a bonus is real money for a goal this year — but it does make the trade visible. Our hourly-versus-salary comparison uses the same pricing logic for offers, and the salary increase calculator prices any raise in dollars.

If You Will Owe: Fix It Before December

The worker in the shortfall example — $150,000 salary, $30,000 bonus, $600 owed — can fix the bill before it becomes one, and the fix costs nothing extra: it just moves money that would be owed in April into withholding now. Three steps, in order:

  1. Step 1 — Project the year. Add salary, bonus, and any other income, subtract the $16,100 standard deduction, and run the brackets. The gap between the real federal tax on the bonus and the 22% withheld is the shortfall — $600 here.
  2. Step 2 — Spread it over the remaining paychecks. Six biweekly checks left in the year means $100 per check. File a new Form W-4 with $100 on line 4(c) (extra withholding per pay period) and the shortfall closes by year-end.
  3. Step 3 — Or make an estimated payment. If no paychecks remain, pay the IRS directly before January 15. Either route avoids the underpayment penalty, which the safe harbors also guard: paying 90% of this year's tax, or 100% of last year's tax (110% if last year's adjusted gross income was over $150,000), is generally enough. Wage withholding is treated as paid evenly through the year even when it is added late, which is why the W-4 route is usually the safer of the two.

Use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator after any large bonus to check the full-year picture, including a spouse's income — the estimator is free and takes a few minutes with your latest pay stubs in hand.

How to Use the Calculator

Price your own bonus in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Enter your salary and the bonus in the paycheck calculator, with your pay frequency, so the tool shows the combined check the way the aggregate method sees it.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the two methods — the percentage method's flat 22% against the aggregate result — and use the higher figure when budgeting, so the deposit never surprises you.
  3. Step 3 — Add your state rate if your state withholds on bonuses, and check your year-to-date Social Security wages to see whether the $184,500 base changes your FICA.
  4. Step 4 — Reconcile before you spend it — compare the 22% withheld with your marginal rate, and if you will owe, set the W-4 extra withholding now rather than at filing.

Limitations

  1. Federal only unless stated: the worked examples use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. State and local taxes are excluded except where a section prices them, so actual take-home is lower in most states.
  2. Withholding methods vary by employer: your employer chooses the percentage or aggregate method per payment, and payroll software follows the published Publication 15-T tables — your exact cents may differ by a few dollars from the figures here.
  3. State supplemental rates change: the California and New York rates in this guide are withholding rates reported for 2026; verify yours with your state revenue department before budgeting, because states can also apply normal W-4 tables instead.
  4. The 401(k) trade depends on your plan: deferral percentages, bonus eligibility, and employer-match rules vary by plan, and the annual contribution limit caps total deferrals.
  5. Self-employed workers are different: this guide covers W-2 employees. Business profit, draws, and contractor payments use estimated tax and self-employment tax rules instead of bonus withholding.
  6. Not tax or legal advice: the take-home sketches use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. Credits, other income, filing status, and multiple jobs change your real return.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about how bonuses are taxed:

Why was my bonus taxed at 22%?

Because the IRS classifies bonuses as supplemental wages, and the standard withholding method for separately paid supplemental wages is a flat 22% federal rate (IRS Publication 15, Section 7). That 22% is withholding — a prepayment, not your final tax rate. Your actual tax on the bonus is set by your marginal bracket when you file: at a $65,000 salary, the real federal tax on a $10,000 bonus is $2,050, so $150 of the $2,200 withheld comes back as part of your refund.

Will I get my bonus tax back when I file my taxes?

You get back the gap between the 22% withheld and your actual marginal rate on the bonus. If your taxable income keeps you in the 10% or 12% bracket, most of the 22% comes back: on a $5,000 bonus at a $52,000 salary, $500 of the $1,100 withheld is refunded. If your marginal rate is exactly 22%, you roughly break even. If it is 24% or higher, the 22% under-withholds and you owe the difference — $600 on a $30,000 bonus at a $150,000 salary.

Are bonuses taxed at a higher rate than regular salary?

No — bonuses are taxed at exactly the same federal brackets as your salary. What is higher is the withholding: 22% flat on the bonus versus the 10% or 12% marginal rate most workers pay on ordinary pay. That gap is why a bonus feels heavily taxed on payday and then partly comes back at filing. The one exception is very large bonuses: supplemental wages above $1 million in a calendar year are withheld at 37%.

How much tax is taken out of a $5,000 bonus?

Under the percentage method with no state tax and wages below the Social Security wage base: $1,100 federal withholding (22%), $310 Social Security (6.2%), and $72.50 Medicare (1.45%) — $1,482.50 total, leaving $3,517.50 in your bank account. The real federal tax depends on your salary: at $52,000 it is only $600, so $500 comes back at filing and the bonus is truly worth $4,017.50. In a state with its own supplemental rate, such as California at 10.23%, another $511.50 comes off, leaving $3,006.00.

Is Social Security tax taken out of a bonus?

Yes, at the same 6.2% employee rate as regular pay — until your year-to-date Social Security wages reach the 2026 wage base of $184,500. After that, no more Social Security tax is withheld from the bonus, or from anything else that year. If a $5,000 bonus arrives when you are already at $182,500, only the $2,000 below the line is taxed: $124 instead of $310, and you keep $186 more. Medicare at 1.45% applies to the whole bonus with no cap, plus 0.9% additional Medicare once wages pass $200,000.

Can I put my bonus in my 401(k) to pay less tax on it?

Yes, if your plan allows it and you elect it before the bonus is paid. Deferring 10% of a $10,000 bonus sends $1,000 to your 401(k) and cuts federal withholding from $2,200 to $1,980, because the 22% applies to the $9,000 left. Cash in hand falls to $6,255 instead of $7,035 — $780 less now — but $1,000 lands in retirement, so you are $220 ahead overall. FICA still applies to the full $10,000, and some plans cap the percentage you can defer from a bonus, so check your plan rules first.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • A $10,000 bonus at a $65,000 salary keeps $7,035 on payday — $2,200 federal withholding, $620 Social Security, $145 Medicare — and $150 comes back at filing, for a true value of $7,185.
  • 22% is withholding, not your tax rate — your marginal bracket decides the refund or the bill: 12% means money back, 24% means money owed.
  • The aggregate method withholds more on the same bonus — $1,150.54 vs $1,100 on a $5,000 bonus — because the tables annualize the combined check; the extra $50.54 returns at filing.
  • A December bonus can dodge Social Security tax — only the part below the $184,500 wage base is taxed at 6.2%, which kept $186 more on a $5,000 bonus at $182,500 year-to-date.
  • Deferring 10% of a $10,000 bonus to a 401(k) puts you $220 ahead — $6,255 cash plus $1,000 in retirement beats $7,035 cash — but FICA still applies to the full bonus.
  • A $5,000 bonus and a $5,000 raise are worth the same $3,667.50 in year one — but the raise repeats every year and the bonus does not, a $14,670 gap over five years.
  • If you will owe, fix it in December — $600 owed on a $30,000 bonus at $150,000 closes with $100 of extra W-4 withholding on each of six remaining paychecks.
  • State tax is the hidden layer — California's 10.23% supplemental rate takes another $511.50 off a $5,000 bonus, leaving $3,006.00 instead of $3,517.50.

Sources & Method

All figures use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction: standard deduction $16,100, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700, 24% to $201,775 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32; supplemental-wage withholding 22% flat to $1 million of cumulative supplemental wages and 37% above, per IRS Publication 15, Section 7 and 26 CFR 31.3402(g)-1; FICA 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%, additional Medicare 0.9% above $200,000 in wages from one employer). Aggregate-method figures use the Publication 15-T percentage method: annualize the combined biweekly check, compute annual tax, divide by 26 — payroll software follows the published tables, so exact cents may differ by a few dollars. State supplemental rates (California 10.23% on bonuses, New York about 11.7%) are withholding rates reported for 2026; verify with your state revenue department. This article is general information, not tax or legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The 22% on your bonus is withholding, not your tax rate — a $10,000 bonus at a $65,000 salary keeps $7,035 on payday and $150 comes back at filing.
  2. Your marginal rate decides the outcome: below 22% you get a refund, at 22% you break even, above 22% you owe — and the aggregate method withholds about $50 more on a $5,000 bonus.
  3. A bonus is one year of a raise, not the raise itself — the same $5,000 is worth $3,667.50 either way in year one, but the raise repeats and the bonus does not.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 5, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
